To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the action of the drugs on normal organ growth was found to be dependent upon both the dose and the duration of treatment.

the action of anti-tumour agents on normal organ and tissue growth can be used as a model for the prediction of their organotoxic side effects and that the inhibition of normal organ and body weight gain is influenced by the loss in appetite and by the decrease of food utilisation.

1. the action of some anti-cancer drugs on normal growth is not necessarily correlated with their anti-cancer activity; 2. some anti-cancer agents are more toxic to normal growth than others; 3. the action of anti-cancer drugs can be modulated by some drugs that affect the normal growth.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new method of drug evaluation, which is based on the use of the growth curves of the normal organ as a model of the growth curves obtained in the tumour-bearing animal.
the design of a cancer chemotherapy which is tailored to the individual patient.
a new approach to chemotherapy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the anti-cancer drugs are not selective and the spectrum of organotoxicity of a particular drug is a good indicator of the anti-tumor spectrum.
the spectrum of anti-tumour action and that of the inhibition of normal body growth of the anti-tumor drugs tested are not necessarily identical, but they are correlated.
the anti-tumours drugs tested, with few exceptions, are not selective in their organotoxicity and that, therefore, the search for new and more selective drugs should be continued.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the drugs which inhibit normal growth and the growth of tumours in rats have a common mechanism of action.
the drugs which inhibit tumours in vivo are also able to inhibit growth of the normal tissues.
the anti-tumoral activity of some of the drugs tested is not necessarily connected with their toxicity to normal tissues and organs.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the anti-tumoral activity of the drug is not necessarily a function of the drug’s cytotoxicity, but rather the drug’s ability to selectively inhibit the growth of the tumor cells.
the anti-tumoral effect of drugs is not always related to their toxicity, which is a common belief.
, in the absence of a specific target, the anti-tumoral activity is often accompanied by a parallel inhibition of the growth of some normal tissues.
